Q: How do HTML landmarks, headings and forms create an accessible document?
A:
Semantic HTML gives browsers and assistive technology meaningful structure before scripts run. Use heading levels to reflect hierarchy, landmarks to identify major regions, labels to name controls and real form elements to provide expected interaction.

A button activates an action; a link navigates to a resource. Custom attributes cannot repair every incorrect native element choice. Validate that important content and actions remain understandable when styling fails, keyboard input replaces a pointer, or JavaScript has not loaded.
Why: A visible placeholder disappears after typing and may not supply a durable accessible name. A label linked to the input remains available while an error message can be associated separately.
Risk: A visually polished page can still lack names, landmarks or keyboard-operable controls.
Trade: Native semantics reduce custom interaction code and improve predictable behavior.
Try: Complete a form using only a keyboard and inspect its accessible names and error relationships.

Q: How do the CSS cascade, box model and layout systems determine the final page?
A:
The cascade resolves competing declarations through origin, importance, layers, specificity and order; layout then uses computed sizes and constraints. The box model distinguishes content, padding, border and margin.

Flexbox distributes items primarily along one dimension, while grid arranges two-dimensional tracks. A child can overflow when an intrinsic minimum size exceeds the available track, even if the parent appears responsive. Inspect computed styles and container constraints before adding arbitrary fixed widths or hiding overflow.
Why: A code block inside a grid cell may force horizontal page scrolling. Allow the cell to shrink with min-width:0 and keep the code block itself scrollable rather than clipping the text from users.
Risk: Hiding overflow can conceal required content and keyboard focus.
Trade: Flexible layouts need explicit content bounds and representative long-text checks.

Q: How do JavaScript closures and event listeners cause stale values or memory retention?
A:
A closure retains access to values in its lexical environment. An event listener remains reachable through its owner until removed or that owner is collected.

Combining long-lived listeners with captured state can retain obsolete data or repeatedly act on a stale snapshot. Install listeners at a clear lifecycle boundary, remove them with the same registered function where required, and deliberately choose whether a handler needs the current state or the state when it was created. Garbage collection cannot free reachable listeners merely because their business task ended.
Why: Navigating between views can install three resize handlers if each mount adds one and cleanup does nothing. All three may run, with older handlers referencing detached view state.
Risk: Duplicate handlers can create repeated effects and growing retained memory.
Trade: Central event ownership simplifies cleanup; local handlers clarify view-specific behavior.
Try: Mount and unmount a view repeatedly and verify that one event triggers one current handler.

Q: How do promises, async/await and Promise.all handle failure?
A:
A promise represents eventual fulfillment or rejection; async/await makes sequencing explicit without removing those failure states. Promise.all rejects when one input rejects but does not automatically cancel the remaining operations.

Promise.allSettled observes every outcome when partial results are meaningful. Decide which operations are independent, which share an effect boundary and which must be cancelled after failure. A catch handler should translate or recover from a known error, not silently convert every failure into successful empty data.
Why: Three independent lookups can finish with two successes and one failure. A dashboard may show partial sections with explicit errors, whereas an all-or-nothing checkout cannot treat the same pattern as a successful complete transaction.
Risk: Rejected aggregation does not imply that sibling side effects stopped.
Trade: Parallel work reduces waiting when independent; explicit sequencing preserves real dependencies.
Try: Demonstrate that a sibling operation still runs after Promise.all rejects.

Q: How does TypeScript narrowing differ from runtime validation?
A:
TypeScript checks source-level assumptions and erases most type information during compilation. Narrowing uses control flow and discriminants to refine possible types inside the checked program. An external JSON response begins as an untrusted value even if a cast tells the compiler otherwise.

Validate its shape and semantic fields before constructing trusted state. Use a discriminated union to represent meaningful states such as loading, ready and failed, so impossible combinations are harder to express. The server must still enforce its own contract.
Why: Casting a response to User does not prove that response.name exists. A malformed response can reach rendering unless runtime validation rejects it and produces a visible error state.
Risk: Type assertions can silence the very boundary uncertainty the program needs to handle.
Trade: Static types reduce internal mistakes; runtime parsers guard external representations.
Try: Parse unknown input into a success/error union without using an unchecked cast.

Q: How do React state, derived values and stable keys prevent inconsistent interfaces?
A:
State should store the minimal information needed to represent user intent and asynchronous results. Derive values that can be computed from current inputs instead of maintaining duplicate state that can disagree.

React keys identify sibling elements across renders; a stable entity identity preserves the intended component association when lists reorder. Array-position keys can attach local state to the wrong item. State updates apply to render snapshots, so use an updater when the next value depends on the previous value.
Why: Reordering editable rows keyed by array index can make one person's unsaved text appear under another person's name. A stable row identifier associates the local input state with the correct entity.
Risk: Duplicated derived state can display a total inconsistent with its line items.
Trade: Minimal state simplifies invariants; controlled local state supports explicit editing workflows.
Try: Reorder a list with an edited row and verify that its value follows the entity.

Q: When is a React effect necessary, and how should it clean up asynchronous work?
A:
An effect synchronizes a rendered component with an external system such as a subscription or network resource. Pure calculations belong in rendering or a deliberate memoized computation, and user-triggered effects often belong in event handlers.

Cleanup should release subscriptions and invalidate obsolete asynchronous ownership. Aborting a fetch can save resources, while an identity or generation check also prevents an old completion from overwriting a newer view. Account for development lifecycle checks and avoid assuming setup runs exactly once forever.
Why: A user changes from account A to B while A's response is delayed. The UI must not render A's result under B even if abort arrives too late to stop A's completion.
Risk: Cancellation alone may not establish current-result ownership.
Trade: Effects are useful for synchronization but add lifecycle and dependency obligations.
Try: Delay an old response and prove it cannot overwrite a newer account view.

Q: How do frontend tests distinguish visual appearance from usable behavior?
A:
A screenshot records pixels for one state and viewport; it does not prove keyboard operation, correct accessible names, race handling or safe rendering of hostile text. Test the user-visible contract through real interactions where practical.

Include loading, empty, error, cancellation and stale-response states, not only a successful populated view. Automated accessibility tools catch a useful subset of issues, while manual keyboard and assistive-technology review answer different questions. Keep assertions on meaningful outcomes rather than component internals.
Why: A button may look enabled in a screenshot but be unreachable by keyboard or trigger the action twice. A browser interaction can verify focus, activation, disabled state and one accepted operation.
Risk: Passing visual snapshots can coexist with inaccessible or incorrect interactions.
Trade: Choose targeted behavioral checks and visual review according to the failure being prevented.
Try: Test submission using a keyboard and simulate a slow response followed by navigation.
